Executive summary 
The findings show a substantial stock of UgIFT assets supporting health care and secondary education, 
alongside equipment and buildings requiring attention. Facilities reported improvements in their 
services, but unfinished works, equipment out of use and weaknesses in asset identification limit the 
benefits. The report sets out the action needed to maintain the assets, complete outstanding works and 
resolve errors in the financial and custody records. 
A total of 229,024 asset records were identified. Schools account for 145,256 and Health Centres for 
63,432. A further 16,663 relate to ministries and agencies, 602 to regional blood banks, 3,067 to 
hospitals under local governments and four to other local -government locations. The total includes 
items whose receipt, classification or programme assign ment still requires confirmation. These cases 
must be resolved before the full population can be certified as physically verified UgIFT assets. 
Overall, 215,504 items (94.1%) are classified Functional and 13,520 (5.9%) Faulty, with the same 
numbers recorded as in use and out of use, respectively. Reasons for non -use include lack of power, 
unfinished buildings, missing parts and insufficient training. These require different responses. Usable 
tag details are unavailable for 178,695 items, making identification and custody checks a substantial 
task. 
Facilities reported improvements in services following UgIFT support. Of 284 health -centre 
respondents, 238 (83.8%) reported at least one benefit, including improved maternity services, access 
to care and use of equipment. Of 193 school respondents, 144 (74.6%) reported benefits such as better 
learning conditions and access to secondary education. These are the facilities’ accounts of changes in 
their services; the exercise did not measure how much of each change was caused by the programme. 
The programme list contains 629 distinct facility entries. Supporting returns account for 590, while 39 
have discrepancies requiring reconciliation. The reviewed evidence identifies at least 70 facilities with 
incomplete works and 13 others awaiting handov er or commissioning. Some facilities were operating 
while particular buildings or supporting structures remained unfinished. Completion, handover and 
readiness for use therefore need to be confirmed separately.

6 
 
Priority actions 
MoFPED and the responsible institutions should first confirm when assets were placed in service. Of 
201,066 full service dates, 3,345 precede programme approval on 27 June 2017. A further 27,958 entries 
contain partial dates or text, which cannot be accept ed as exact service dates. The review also found 
787 purchase dates later than the recorded service date. These findings overlap. Each affected date 
should be checked against receipt, acceptance or commissioning records, together with the asset’s 
ownership and programme assignment. 
Where a full service date cannot be supported, retain the reported period or status in the supporting 
records and leave the exact -date field blank until it is confirmed. A purchase date or the programme 
start date should not be used to fill the gap. Approve supported corrections before migration to IFMIS 
and recalculate depreciation and net book value where the corrected dates affect them. 
Available recorded costs total UGX 996.813 billion, with costs missing for 1,086 records. Net book 
value remains unresolved for 23,016 records. For the 180,730 recognized records with complete 
accounting figures, cost of UGX 760.987 billion less accumulated depreciation of UGX 165.185 billion 
gives a net book value of UGX 595.802 billion at 30 September 2026. Net book value is the recorded 
cost remaining after depreciation; it does not measure the asset’s market value or physical condition. 
Cost evidence also needs review. Costs for 166,593 items were estimated by comparison with similar 
assets. These account for 82.44% of available recorded cost. Of 298 construction -in-progress entries, 
275 have zero cost and four have no cost recorded. The recorded amounts therefore cannot establish the 
full value of unfinished works. Obtain the supporting expenditure or valuation records, resolve missing 
amounts and approve changes before treating the balances as a verified programme valuation. 
Facility managers, local governments and the responsible ministries should give priority to essential 
equipment, reliable power and water, user training and outstanding buildings. Keep an action list 
naming the item or facility, the responsible officer and the agreed completion date. Assess faulty items 
for repair, replacement or disposal, and review the 22,161 fully depreciated records still marked in use. 
Reconcile delivery, transfer and custody records before concluding that an asset is missing. The 
recommendations and appendices provide the specific cases and follow-up required.

1 Introduction and background 
1.1 Introduction 
This report presents the findings of the UgIFT asset verification undertaken by the Ministry of Finance, 
Planning and Economic Development as part of programme closure activities. It sets out the status of 
the assets provided by the programme to the target ed national institutions responsible for supporting 
the implementation of the programme, Blood Banks and local governments specifically targeting Seed 
Secondary Schools and health facilities upgraded from Health Centre II to Health Centre III.  
1.2 Background to the verification 
The Uganda Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfers (UgIFT) Programme is a government programme 
implemented through a Programme -for-Results (PforR) launched and aligned with the broader IGFT 
Reform Programme (2015). UgIFT 1.0 began with US$200 million in FY2017/ 18, supporting 
Education and Health. This was later expanded through additional financing of US$300 million, 
including US$240 million in credit and US$60 million in grants, with US$50 million from the IDA 
Refugee Support Window, expanding beyond Education and Health to water and Environment and 
Agriculture (micro-scale irrigation) making the overall funding total of US$500 million.  
The Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfer Reform Programme (IGFT RP) was revised in 2020 to align 
with the Third National Development Plan (NDP III 2020/21 - 2024/25), and to directly contribute to 
Four (04) Programmes i.e. Human Capital Development; Public Se ctor Transformation; Natural 
Resources, Environment, Climate change, Land and Water Management; and Development Plan 
Implementation.  
Overall, the development objective of the UgIFT Programme was to: “Improve the adequacy, equity, 
and effectiveness of financing and the oversight, management, and delivery of Local Government 
services in Education, Health, Water and Environment, and Agricu lture (micro -scale irrigation), 
including refugees and their host communities”.  
Specifically, the Programme sought to:  
1. Increase the adequacy and predictability of fiscal transfers to Local Governments for service 
delivery;  
2. Improve the equity and transparency of allocation mechanisms through the introduction of 
formula-based transfers;  
3. Strengthen performance incentives and accountability systems for Local Governments; and  
4. Expand access to quality education and health infrastructure, particularly in under-served areas. 
The UgIFT Programme had four components aimed at strengthening the intergovernmental fiscal 
transfer system while supporting investments in service delivery infrastructure. These included; 
Component 1: Reform of the Intergovernmental Fiscal Transfer System 
This supported the design and implementation of a reformed fiscal transfer framework based on 
objective and transparent allocation criteria. This resulted into introduction of formula -based grants - 
Revised allocation formulas reflecting population, infrastructure gaps, and service delivery needs. 
Component 2: Education Infrastructure Development 
This component financed the construction and upgrading of education facilities, particularly 
government secondary schools in under-served sub-counties. This involved construction and equipping 
of new secondary schools - classrooms, laboratories, administra tion blocks, sanitation facilities, 
teachers’ houses, furniture and ICT equipment in the different local governments.

8 
 
Component 3: Health Infrastructure Development 
This supported investments in health facilities to improve access to primary health care services at the 
local level. The major outputs under the component were construction and upgrading of health centers 
- Staff accommodation, sanitation facilities and provision of medical equipment. 
Component 4: Local Government Performance and Institutional Strengthening 
This aimed at strengthening LG capacity in planning, budgeting, procurement, and infrastructure 
management. Under this component, annual Local Government P erformance Assessments have been 
undertaken across the 176 L Gs, capacity building and technical support strengthened monitoring a nd 
reporting systems.  
The Programme was implemented through a clearly defined results framework that connected actions 
and incentives across three levels of government to strengthen service delivery outcomes. The 
programme came to an end on 31 December 2025. The following areas of support describe the following 
outputs under the different components; current asset and facility findings ar e presented later in this 
report. 
1. Budget Support 
a) Education: 196 of 259 Seed Secondary Schools are complete of which 189 are operational.  
b) Health: 354 of 373 health facilities, upgrades/new constructions (HC II to HC III) are complete. 
c) Water and Environment: 758 - piped water systems, 5,398- point water sources, 7,082 water 
supply systems rehabilitated, 325 designs completed, and 256 sanitation facilities in the targeted 
service units. 
d) Agriculture (Micro -scale Irrigation): Over 6,235 irrigation systems were installed (4,843 
hectares under irrigation), 632 irrigation demonstration sites in 135 LGs set up. 
e) Refugee intervention: 51 primary schools and  35 health facilities in refugee hosting districts 
(RHD) were transitioned and integrated into the LG service. 
f) Blood Banks: Regional Blood Banks in Arua and Hoima were completed and commissioned 
while Soroti Regional Blood Bank was rehabilitated.  
2. Grant management  
Assets for institutional strengthening and retooling including ICT equipment and vehicles were 
provided. The Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic Development (MoFPED) through PFM 
Coordination Unit (RCU) manages the Government of Uganda counterpart funding of the programme 
to support the grant management component of the UgIFT programme. The grant management supports 
in financing of Central Government actions intended to achieve programme objectives and 
Disbursement Linked Indicators (DLIs). To this en d, MoFPED through RCU supported MDAs to 
acquire different assets meant to support programme implementation.  
1.3 Justification 
The UgIFT programme came to an end on 31st December 2025. As part of the programme’s closure 
activities, MoFPED, through RCU, commissioned an end-of-programme asset verification exercise to 
take stock of the assets procured under the programme and to estab lish where those assets were, how 
they were being used as part of the processes to hand them over to government for sustainability 
purposes.  
1.4 Objectives of the assignment 
The objective of the assignment was to undertake verification and recording of all assets acquired under 
the UgIFT Programme. Specifically, the assignment intended to;

9 
 
a) Identify and verify the existence of the assets 
b) Verify the assets condition and status: specifically, the condition on functionality, 
usage/performance and location among others 
c) Assess financial management aspects: residual value of the investments/hardware/tools for 
purposes of financial reporting for project closure 
d) List the assets that are obsolete, unserviceable and require disposal 
e) Develop a computerized database of the investment/hardware/tools to facilitate recording of 
new deployed assets/investments. 
f) Undertake PFM Assessment on Asset Management practices (including sustainability, 
Operations and Maintenance) of the UgIFT implementing LGs  
1.5 Scope of Work 
The assignment covered institutions at national and local government level that directly implemented 
the UgIFT programme through coordination, support and implementation. At local government level, 
the study focused on upgraded health facilities and Seed Secondary Schools that received assets under 
the programme. Health Centers and other local-government assets are also reported separately. 
Specifically, the assignment involved the following tasks;   
a) Verification of the Asset’s Records of targeted ministries departments and agencies and local 
governments  
b) Physical and Functional Verification of assets 
c) Data Consolidation for generation of a single data base of assets provided by the program 
d) Generation of an IFMIS ready Asset Register for Integration, and Migration into IFMIS  
e) Review of the UgIFT Asset Management Practices 
1.6 Expected deliverables 
Key expected outputs of the consultant include: 
a) Report with the list and current status of assets acquired under the programmes; 
b) An automated up-to-date assets data base of UgIFT Investments across MDALGs; 
c) Report on the estimated value of assets under the programme as well as operations and maintenance 
arrangements; 
d) IFMIS-Ready Asset Register and Data Migration Report 
e) Report on functionality of assets relating to systems investments; 
f) Report on Assessment of Asset Management Practices, Risks and recommendations.

2 Approach and methodology 
The verification exercise was conducted using a participatory and consultative process and implemented 
in three interlinked phases: Preparatory and inception phase, Data collection phase and the report 
writing phase.  
2.1 Preparation 
After signing of the contract, the assignment commenced with an entry meeting on 28th May 2026. 
During this meeting, the Client specified target MDAs to be visited, the LG stakeholders to be reached 
as well as the documents to be reviewed. The Inception ph ase was completed and the inception report 
submitted on 18th June, 2026 which provided an agreed scope, approach and work plan for the exercise.  
2.2 Pilot Test 
The team also undertook a pilot test in Wakiso District Local Government, with verification carried out 
at Buloba Health Centre III a nd Sumbwe Seed Secondary School. During the pilot test, it was found 
out that, among others, there are cases of mismatches of facility names, that UgIFT assets can be 
integrated into the general LG asset register. This facilitated improving the design of the data collection 
process including; design of data collection tools, determining the timeline for data collection and 
estimated costs. 
2.3 Data collection 
This exercise was undertaken in two phases first at National level and later at the Local government 
level.  
National level: Physical visits to verify assets provided by the programme at the national -level was 
completed on the 19th of August 2026. This covered 15 MDAs including; Ministry of Works and 
Transport (MoWT); Ministry of Education and Sports (MoES); Ministry of Agricu lture, Animal 
Industries and Fisheries (MAAIF); Ministry of Health (MoH); Office of the Prime Minister (OPM); 
Ministry of Water and Environment (MoWE); Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development 
(MoGLSD); Local Government Finance Commission; Nationa l Environment Management Authority 
(NEMA); Public Procurement and Disposal of Assets Authority (PPDA); Office of the Auditor General 
(OAG); Ministry of Public Service (MoPs); Ministry of Lands, Housing and Urban Development 
(MoLHUD); Ministry of Local Government (MoLG) and Ministry of Finance, Planning and Economic 
Development (MoFPED). Additionally, three Blood Banks of Hoima, Arua and Soroti were covered. 
Local government level: The local government verification targeted UgIFT upgraded or constructed 
Health Centres and Seed Secondary Schools. The programme reconciliation list contains 629 distinct 
entries: 371 Health Centres and 258 schools under 160 recorded local government names. The process 
began with training of field teams prior to the actual field verification. 
Training of field teams:  A total of 85 Research Assistants (RAs) and 7 Regional Supervisors were 
trained. The training took place from 21st to 23rd August 2026 while physical verification started on the 
24th of August 2026. During the asset verification, the RAs visited Seed Secondary Schools , Health 
Centres and Blood Banks.  
Physical verification: This exercise commenced on the 24 th of August 2026 and was completed on 
17th September 2026. The local government physical verification involved entry meetings with the LG 
leadership at the LG headquarters for authorization and review of reports relating to UgIFT assets, key 
informant interviews with the technical teams especially the Chief Administrative Officers, Finance 
Officers, District Health Officers and District Education Officers. Thereafter, the RAs proceeded to the 
facilities for physical verification of the assets.

11 
 
At local government level, the programme list had 629 facilities: 371 Health Centres and 258 Seed 
Secondary Schools. The list recorded 547 facilities (87.0%) as complete and 82 (13.0%) as ongoing. 
The ongoing works were more common among Seed Secondary Schools (63, or 24.4%) than among 
Health Centres (19, or 5.1%).  
2.4 Quality assurance 
Regional supervisors checked daily field activity and reviewed the completed tools. The central 
technical team carried out spot checks and helped resolve operational questions. Teams compared 
institutional asset information with the items and explanations provided during visits, while supervisors 
referred matters requiring clarification to the team leader and field coordinator. 
2.5 Asset categories, condition, use and identification 
Asset categories: Each entry in the Asset Register  represents one recorded unit. The analysis covers 
buildings, ICT equipment, transport equipment, furniture and fittings, medical, laboratory and research 
equipment, other classified assets, items outside fixed -asset classification and unclassified entries. 
Assets are grouped by the institution or beneficiary to which they are attributed.  
Condition and use: Condition and use were reported for each asset during the verification. A working 
asset is one recorded as functional and in use. An asset recorded as faulty was reported as not working 
and not in use. This included assets that were broken down or damaged. An asset that was new and in 
store was recorded as functional but not in use. Additionally, an asset that was held elsewhere, not yet 
delivered or awaiting power installation, completion of buildings or trained users, was also recorded as 
functional but not in use.  
Identification: An asset is properly identified when carried a UgIFT programme marking. However, 
there were other assets that had no UgIFT marking but the officers on ground identified them as UgIFT 
assets.    
2.6 Financial analysis and Valuation 
The Government of Uganda Asset Accounting Policies and Guidelines 2023 was used to determine as 
the policy basis for determining recorded values, depreciation and net book values. Financial values are 
reported as at 30 th September 2026 . Straight -line depreciation was applied w here the required 
information was available.  
2.7 Analysis and reporting 
Analysis and reporting was done through triangulation of the literature from different policy, Planning 
and Financial documents including: Government of Uganda Asset Accounting Policies and Guidelines 
2023; asset registers; asset records at national and lo cal government levels; physical inspections; 
discussions with facility managers; photographs and asset counts for each institution.  
2.8 Challenges and Limitations to the assignment 
a) Difficult terrain and poor physical accessibility of facilities: Physical accessibility presented a 
significant operational challenge especially for facilities located in areas characterised by difficult 
terrain and limited transport accessibility such as Bwesumbu HC III, Bwesumbu Seed School, 
Buhuhira and Kabingo in Kasese District. In addition, accessing facilities within the Island was 
difficult, time consuming and expensive. This led the teams to overshoot the anticipated time for 
data collection.  
b) High transportation cost: Given the national wide coverage, the rising fuel prices led to high field 
costs. The field teams spent more money than was anticipated. The costs were extra ordinarily 
higher for island facilities like Kalangala, Buvuma, Mayuge among others. For instance, Kalangala 
had 3 facilities with long distance on water that required hiring a private boat since it was not a

common route to the transporters and outside the ferry schedules. A similar situation was 
encountered in Buvuma and Namayingo districts.  
c) Poor record keeping: In many LGs and facilities, there were no clear records about the assets 
delivered under UgIFT. The LGs and the facilities had incomplete or missing UgIFT asset registers 
which delayed data collection. Subsequently, the teams took longer in such facilities identifying the 
assets as most of these were not engraved with the UgIFT identifiers while others were not engraved 
at all. In addition, the field teams encountered situations where some Assets could not be physically 
accessed especially for schools since it was holiday time.

3 Findings 
This section presents results of the verification exercise based on the specific objectives. The results are 
presented in different results levels indicating availability of assets, asset condition and functionality, 
asset marking and identification and the financial analysis in each subsection.  
3.1 Overall results  
This section provides an overall view of the UgFT asset status combining both National level agencies 
and schools and health centres.  
1. Overall asset availability  
A total of 229,024 assets are recorded across the targeted MDAs, beneficiary Blood Banks, Upgraded 
Health Centres and Seed Secondary  School. These include vehicles, laptops, printers, desktop 
computers, projectors, cameras, furniture (desks, chairs, tables and stools), UPS systems, digital phones, 
paper shredders, tablets and clinical equipment, among others.  
Overall, the Seed Secondary Schools hold the majority of assets 63.4% (145,256), followed by Health 
Centres with 27.7% (63,432). MDAs hold 7.3% (16,663) and regional Blood Banks with 0.3% (602). 
In addition, some assets were found to have been reallocated by LGs from Health Center to hospital s 
such as Rukoki general hospital in Kasese Municipality.
